Hi everyone. I'm Haoyu Wang from Penn State.

Today I'll talk about our work on exponential quantum advantage in number-on-forehead communication.

This is joint work with Pei Wu, also at Penn State, and Guangxu Yang at the University of Southern California.

Let me first recall the usual two-party communication model.

Alice has an input x, and Bob has an input y.

They communicate by bits to compute a function f of x and y.

They can use public randomness, and the answer must be correct with probability at least two thirds on every input.

We only charge for the communication bits.

Given a protocol, the cost is defined in worst case, over all inputs and random choices

And local computation is free.

In the classical setting, the messages are bits. while in the quantum setting, the messages are qubits.

and We do not assume any prior entanglement.

We write R of f for the smallest cost among all satisfied protocols

this is the randomized communication complexity of f.

And write Q of f for the quantum communication complexity in the same way.

Quantum advantage for two parties has been studied extensively across many models and tasks.

These are just a few examples.

In the two-party model, the inputs are disjoint.

So, what happens when more players have access to overlapping inputs?

F(x,y,z)F(x,y,z)F(x,y,z)

This brings us to the number-on-forehead model.

Here we have three inputs, x, y, and z, and three players: Alice, Bob, and Charlie.

Imagine that each input is written on one player's forehead. Everyone can see the other two inputs, but cannot see their own.

So Alice sees y and z, Bob sees x and z, and Charlie sees x and y. Their goal is to compute a function F of all three inputs x,y and z.

The question

Quantum advantage in the NOF model?

Alice sees y,z\cy{y},\cz{z}y,z
Bob sees x,z\cx{x},\cz{z}x,z
Charlie sees x,y\cx{x},\cy{y}x,y
The strongest classical model
overlapping inputs and arbitrary interaction
Can exponential quantum advantage
survive in the NOF model?
[Gavinsky–Pudlák, CCC 2008]

With overlapping inputs and unrestricted interaction, NOF is the strongest classical model.

So, a natural question is:

Can exponential quantum advantage survive in the NOF model?

This question is also asked by Garvinsky and Pudlak in 2000 and 8.

Our result

Our answer: yes

Theorem
There is an explicit partial Boolean function F:({0,1}n)3→{0,1}F:(\{0,1\}^n)^3\to\{0,1\}F:({0,1}n)3→{0,1} such that
quantum communication
QNOF(F)=O(log⁡n)\QQ^{\NOF}(F)=O(\log n)QNOF(F)=O(logn)
vs.
randomized communication
RNOF(F)=Ω~(n1/32)\RR^{\NOF}(F)=\tO\big(n^{1/32}\big)RNOF(F)=Ω(n1/32)
the quantum protocol
never uses the overlap of the inputs
the lower bound allows the full NOF view
and unrestricted interaction

Our answer is yes.

We construct an explicit partial Boolean function on three n-bit inputs.

It has a quantum protocol using only logarithmic communication,

while every randomized NOF protocol needs polynomial communication.

One feature I want to emphasize is that our quantum protocol does not need the overlap between the players' inputs. We will show the quantum protocol later.

The classical lower bound, however, allows the full NOF view and unrestricted interaction.

SMP: simultaneous message passing

Quantum advantage in the NOF model has also attracted a lot of attention.

Gavinsky and Pudlák studied a non-interactive setting.

Yang and Zhang studied simultaneous message passing, or SMP, and one-way communication.

Pei and I gave a partial-function separation in a conservative one-way model, where the last player's input access is restricted.

However, an exponential quantum advantage in the general unrestricted NOF model remained out of reach until our work.

We obtain such a separation for a partial Boolean function.

Let me briefly mention why classical NOF lower bounds are interesting beyond this separation.

One major motivation comes from circuit complexity.

For suitable functions and communication models, sufficiently strong NOF lower bounds imply circuit lower bounds.

There are also connections to pseudorandom generators, streaming, cryptography, and other areas.

We can encode the bit strings into unitary matrices with finite precision and negligible error.

Our starting point is a two-party problem studied by Aruna~cha~lam, Gir~ish, and Lifshitz.

Alice has two unitary matrices, A and C, and Bob has B and D. Here m is the matrix dimension.

They want to know whether the real part of the trace of A times B times C times D is large or small.

This quantity is promised to be at least point nine or at most point one.

They proposed a quantum protocol using only log m qubits, while proved that every randomized protocol needs at least Omega the square root of m bits.

I'll describe the matrices as exact unitaries. Because we can endcode the bit strings to unitaries by finite-precision encoding and it only introduces negligible errors.

Here we briefly introduce the quantum protocol for ABCD problem.

v is a random unit vector and describes a pure state in this mixture.

a controlled operation applies a matrix U to v only when the first qubit is one.

Alice first applies controlled A dagger and sends the whole system to Bob.

Bob applies controlled B dagger and sends it back.

They do the same for C dagger and D dagger.

Bob measures the first qubit in the Hadamard basis.

The probability of plus

is one half plus the normalized real trace divided by two.

This gives probabilities at least point nine five and at most point five five in the two cases.

They repeat a constant number of times and use major voting to improve the success probability.

So it gives a bounded error protocol with logarithmic communication cost.

We call the problem Interleaved Unitary Product.

There are ten unitary matrices from A one to E two. They are grouped into three blocks.

X contains the four A and C matrices, Y contains the four B and D matrices, and Z contains E one and E two.

The players have the usual NOF views.

We form P and Q, each by multiplying four matrices in the ABCD product. Then use P and Q as factors in a second product, W equals P times E one times Q times E two.

The task is again to determine whether normalized trace is large or small.

Following the quantum protocol of the ABCD problem, here we present the protocol for IUP briefly.

For example, Charlie can see the group X matrices A one C one A two C two,

and Alice the Y matrices, and Bob the Z matrices.

Starting with the same initial state, they apply the controlled operation in the order of the written product, from A one dagger to E two dagger.

After each operation, they pass the whole system to the player responsible for the next factor.

Again, the last player applies the same measurement.

There are constantly many repetitions.

constantly many messages

Each message costs logarithmic qubits,

so the total communication is logarithmic.

The classical lower bound

Three obstacles

1
Input overlap
a third player who sees both inputs can make a hard two-party problem trivial
2
Unrestricted interaction
lower bounds for one-way or SMP protocols do not carry over
3
randomized LBquantum LB
discrepancy
Lack of tools
discrepancy bounds also lower-bound quantum communication, so they cannot give the separation

Ok, Let's move on the lower bound sides.

There are three obstacles.

First, input overlap can make a hard two-party problem easy in NOF model.

Second, a one-way or SMP lower bound does not rule out a short interactive protocol.

Third, the general discrepancy methods also give quantum lower bounds, so they cannot prove the quantum vs classical separation.

Now let’s look at a key object in the lower bound analysis, called cylinder intersection.

Fix the public randomness and a candidate transcript tau.

We look at the sets of inputs producing tau.

For Alice, whether the messages agree with tau depends only on her view, Y and Z.

It does not depend on X.

The inputs of this condition form a cylinder in the X direction.

Bob and Charlie give two more cylinders in the same way.

An input produces tau exactly when all three conditions hold,

so these inputs form an intersection.

Its indicator is the product of three Boolean functions, one for each player's view.

This gives a useful way to analyse any protocol.

A protocol cost at most t bits partitions the input space into at most two to the t cylinder intersections.

Idea: to prove a short protocol cannot create this acceptance gap

Ok. Let's continue.

We define two input distributions.

Under mu zero, all ten matrices are independent Haar-random unitaries.

Under mu one, we sample the first nine independently, then choose E two to be the inverse of P times E one times Q.

This forces W to equal the identity, so every such input is a one-input.

Under mu zero, W is Haar random. With high probability it has small normalized real trace.

So almost all inputs are zero-inputs.

We denote the cylinder intersections on which a protocol outputs one by P.

These cylinder intersections must have large probability under mu one and small probability under mu zero.

And the lower bound will come from showing that a short protocol cannot create this acceptance gap.

Here is the intuition.

Suppose a cylinder intersection contains a substantial amount of probability under mu one.

We want to show that it must also contain a comparable amount under mu zero.

Then a protocol cannot use just a few accepting transcripts to collect most of the one-inputs

while avoiding most of the zero-inputs.

It means a lot of transcripts , in other words, a lot of communication bits.

Let's make this comparison precise.

The corruption bound

corruption
one-sided, hence weaker
leaves room for a quantum vs. classical separation

This is usually called a corruption bound.

For every cylinder intersection, its mu-one probability is at most a fixed constant alpha times its mu-zero probability, plus an exponentially small error.

Unless its mu-one probability is tiny, it must also contain comparable mu-zero probability.

This one-sided bound is weaker than discrepancy method, leaving room for a quantum–classical separation.

Let's sum the corruption bound over all accepting transcripts, or cylinder intersection.

The cylinder intersections are disjoint, and there are at most two to the t of them.

After averaging over the randomness, the acceptance probability under mu one is close to one, while alpha times the acceptance probability under mu zero is close to zero.

So the accumulated additive error must be at least a constant.

This forces t to be at least polynomial m. and m is about sqrt n.

So, the remaining task is to prove the corruption bound.

Let's first analyze the probability of a cylinder intersection c under mu one.

Write the indicator as f of Y and Z, times g of X and Z, times h of X and Y.

Under mu one, X and Y are independent, but Z depends on them through the product constraint.

To compare it with the probability under mu 0, where all inputs are independent, we need to decouple the correlation between the inputs.

At first, Hölder's inequality separates out h, leaving a high moment of that expectation.

We use a large p moment, rather than just the second moment, because a larger p reduces the loss when h has small density.

The remaining task is to control the dependence between Z and X, Y in this high moment.

For this decoupling purpose, we return to the two-party estimate of Aruna~cha~lam, Gir~ish, and Lifshitz.

Take any Boolean test u on Alice's matrices and any Boolean test w on Bob's matrices.

On the left, the last matrix D is chosen as the inverse of A times B times C, so their product is the identity.

just like mu 1

On the right, all four matrices are independent. like mu zero.

This is the comparison we need, but so far it applies only to two-party tests.

We denote this two-party corruption bound by AGL.

∥f∥U(2,p) 2p = E[∏j=1pf(Y,Z(j)) f(Y′,Z(j))]\displaystyle\gn{\ff}{p}^{\,2p}\ =\ \E\Big[\prod_{j=1}^{p}\ff\big(\Y,\Z^{(j)}\big)\,\ff\big(\Y',\Z^{(j)}\big)\Big]∥f∥U(2,p)2p​ = E[j=1∏p​f(Y,Z(j))f(Y′,Z(j))]
Boolean f\fff: how often is the sampled grid all ones?

The grid norm, from Kelley, Lovett, and Meka, describes these high-order averages.

Think of f as a zero-one table: Y indexes the rows, and Z the columns.

Independently sample two rows and p columns, and multiply the entries.

The average is the grid norm raised to the power two p.

For Boolean f, this average is exactly the probability that every sampled entry is one.

First, expand the high moment using p copies of Z, independent given P and Q. Inner AGL separates the constrained X,Y average into the two averages shown here.

Next, Cauchy–Schwarz separates f from g. Outer AGL removes the conditioning on P and Q and gives the grid norms in the final bound.

Regularity and min-degree[Kelley, Lovett, Meka, STOC 2024]

no unusually sparse rows

Our upper bound under mu one involves grid norms.

We want to express it using densities so that we can compare it with the probability under mu zero.

So we first consider Boolean matrices whose grid norms are close to their densities.

This is the notion of pseudorandomness captured by grid regularity.

Write delta u for the density of a Boolean function u.

Grid regularity bounds the norm by a one-plus-epsilon factor of the density.

Epsilon is a small fixed constant; d is the moment, which we choose later.

The minimum-degree condition says that each row has at least a one-minus-epsilon fraction of the overall density.

The first controls concentration; the second prevents sparse rows. We call a function regular when both conditions hold.

Still to handle: an arbitrary cylinder intersection

First suppose f and g are regular.

We also set aside functions of very small density for now.

Under the independent distribution, a moment estimate of Kelley, Lovett, and Meka uses regularity and minimum degree to show that

the intersection has probability at least a constant times the product of the three densities.

Under mu one, our grid norm bound gives an upper bound comparable to that same product, plus a exponentially small error.

So the two estimates compare the distributions through the product of densities.

This gives the desired corruption bound for the regular case.

But, We still need to handle a general cylinder intersection.

For a general intersection, we adapt a regularity decomposition of Abboud et al in 2024.

It writes the indicator as a sum of disjoint Boolean pieces,

ci equals to f i times g i times h i

each still a cylinder intersection.

Each piece is supported on a smaller product of three input sets.

The local densities on the slide are the averages within these smaller sets.

Every piece either satisfies regular , or has at least one very small local density.

We call the latter pieces sparse.

There are at most exponentially many pieces in polynomial d.

Sparse pieces can be handled without regularity.

For a Boolean function, the grid norm with moment two is at most the square root of its density.

Apply our grid norm bound with moment p equal to two.

In every sparse piece, at least one factor among f,g and h makes the contribution small.

This gives a total sparse contribution exponentially small in d, plus the accumulated errors.

We can now combine the regular and sparse cases.

The regular pieces contribute at most alpha times their total mu-zero probability, plus additive errors.

The sparse pieces contribute an amount exponentially small in d.

Increasing d makes the sparse contribution smaller, but it also increases the number of pieces

and therefore accumulates the error.

We balance these effects by choosing d to be the sixteenth root of m. We didn't try to optimize this constant.

This gives the exponentially small error for our corruption bound.

Summing over accepting transcripts, as we did earlier, it gives the polynomial lower bound.

Let me end with three open questions.

First, what is the true randomized communication complexity of IUP?

It would be interesting to improve our polynomial lower bound and obtain matching classical upper and lower bounds.

` Second, can we prove an exponential separation for more than three players?

The regularity decomposition we use here is specific to three players, so extending that part of the argument is one obstacle.

Third, can we obtain such a separation for a total Boolean function?

The quantum protocol relies on a promise that separates large and small trace values.

Removing the promise while preserving the quantum advantage remains interesting.

Thank you
